transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer, Sofia Lin (Redwood); Dana Brooks, Miguel Santos, Leah Kim (Aurora Financial)

Summary section (auto):
Alex: quick tour of structured output and function calling, also show console Optimize suggestions and Dedicated/VPC options.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. um i'm Alex Mercer, i'm an AE at Redwood. Sofia and I will run through a short demo — structured output (json mode), function/tool calling, and then the console bits around Optimize and rollouts.
[00:18] Dana: Hi Alex, thanks. I'm Dana, Head of AI at Aurora. We brought Miguel and Leah — Miguel runs infra, Leah is on security. We're primarily trying to understand guardrails and how to lock down outputs for downstream systems.
[00:32] Sofia: great, thanks. quick qualification — are you leaning Hosted or Dedicated/private?
[00:38] Miguel: we're leaning Dedicated or Private VPC. We need data residency and KMS integration. Also latency SLOs: sub-200ms median for simple responses, and cost needs to be reasonable.
[00:49] Leah: and SOC2 + audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC — those are must haves.
[00:56] Alex: totally — we'll cover those. quick agenda: 1) show JSON mode with schema enforcement and validation 2) demonstrate function/tool calling and how the runtime guarantees structured output 3) Console Optimize and rollout controls 4) mapping to Dedicated/VPC and security features, then next steps.

[02:02] Sofia (demo): i'll start with the API. here's a sample request in JSON mode — we send a schema with the call: {"order": {"type": "object", "properties": {"id": {"type": "string"}, "amount": {"type": "number"}}, "required": ["id","amount"]}} — and then model returns a json blob matching that shape. the runtime validates and will either return a parseable object or a structured error.
[02:28] Miguel: sorry can you repeat the field types — sometimes these auto transcripts change things; what about enums and nested arrays?
[02:34] Sofia: yeah enums supported, nested arrays fine. we also support strict mode where the model is constrained to the schema and we apply a second-layer parser/validator to prevent hallucinated fields. if a token stream deviates we can fall back to a validation error and optionally call a correction function.
[02:59] Dana: do you run heuristics server-side or is that client-side?
[03:04] Sofia: both. the API accepts the schema, we do server-side validation. you can also configure post-processing hooks on the client or console that auto-correct or flag. and you'll see in Console you can add guardrail policies.

[04:15] Alex: now function/tool calling — i'll show a quick example: we have a tool called charge_customer that accepts {customer_id, amount, currency}; the model can return a function_call in the streaming response and the runtime will emit a structured function invocation rather than free text.
[04:31] Sofia (typing): i'm going to run the demo request — live. (audio: keyboard)
[04:45] [Demo audio glitches, transcription imperfect]
[05:02] Sofia: okay live response — model returned a function_call payload: {"name": "charge_customer", "arguments": {"customer_id": "C-12941", "amount": 345.50, "currency": "USD"}} — the runtime validated against the registered function signature and then forwarded to the tool adapter. you can configure retries and idempotency keys.
[05:32] Miguel: how do you guarantee the function args are safe? i.e. we don't want free text being injected into integers or SQL.
[05:38] Sofia: good question. we register function schemas using an OpenAPI-like signature. the runtime will coerce and validate types; if coercion fails we either return a structured error or call a sanitizer function you provide. additionally, you can enable strict content scanning for PII or SQL patterns before tool execution.

[06:05] Leah: on encryption — KMS/HSM — can Redwood integrate with our key management?
06:11 Miguel: (interrupt) also audit logs for every function call, want to ensure non-repudiation.
[06:16] Alex: yes both. for Private/VPC deployments we support customer-owned KMS via our KMS connector (we call it KMS Bridge in docs, might be named differently in notes). audit logs are exported to your S3 or SIEM with per-request metadata, key ids, and signing. we also support HSM-backed keys on-prem.

[07:02] Sofia: switching to Console — here is the Optimize tab. it analyzes your request distribution and recommends batching, quantization profiles, and model variants to hit your latency/cost target. you'll see a suggestion to apply 8-bit quantization for a high-throughput route and to pin a lower-latency decoder for the chat route.
[07:28] Dana: can Optimize run offline on our prompt set? we need to ensure quality doesn't drop.
[07:34] Sofia: yes, you can upload eval sets and run regressions; Console will show expected token-cost savings and the projected latency impact. you can also tie regressions to alerts so if eval metrics drop we can auto-roll back.

[08:12] Miguel: for the Dedicated pool — what's the isolation? are we sharing nodes?
[08:17] Alex: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools for your workload only. physical isolation depends on the contract: single-tenant racks or logical partitioning. we provide throughput SLAs and options for burst capacity. for strict compliance customers we offer an on-prem bundle with the same control plane APIs.

[09:05] Sofia: back to structured output guardrails — one pattern customers like: send a schema + a small canonical example and enable the "strict_json" flag. runtime will then do a two-stage check: 1) model-level guidance (prompting) 2) parser-level verification and optional automated correction via a registered function that runs in a sandbox. this prevents downstream pipeline crashes.
[09:37] Dana: if the model emits extra fields, does it just drop them?
[09:40] Sofia: depends on policy — console lets you choose: drop unknown fields, reject and return error, or move unknowns to a metadata bucket. most customers choose reject for finance workflows.

[10:12] (Brief silence, keyboard sounds)
[10:35] Sofia: showing a toolchain example: user asks "Create refund for order 12941" — model emits a function_call to refund_order, which triggers an internal microservice. the service returns a status object which we map back to a structured chat message. you can also configure the runtime to call multiple tools (e.g., check_balance -> refund -> notify) with orchestration hooks.
[11:02] Miguel: do you support transactional semantics? if refund fails half-way what happens?
[11:08] Alex: we offer best-effort orchestration with retries and a rollback adapter pattern. for strict transactions you should implement two-phase commit on your service side; the runtime supports idempotency keys and ordered execution.

[11:35] Leah: on the security docs — we need SOC2 type II evidence, network diagrams, and pen test results. also SSO/SAML integration details for RBAC.
[11:44] Sofia: yes we'll send a security pack; it's in our docs hub. it includes SOC2 summary, pen test high-level results, and sample SAML metadata. we'll include a network diagram for the Private deployment.

[12:10] (Demo continues — Sofia toggles Console features)
[13:00] Sofia: now i want to show runtime-level validation working with streaming. even in streaming mode, we can buffer the token stream until we have a parseable json object then emit the function_call. that avoids half-baked calls. there are heuristics to keep latency low.
[13:30] Dana: how often have you seen streaming adversely affect latency?
[13:33] Sofia: rarely; our batching and prefix caching reduce token cost and typically keep cold-starts in check. for high qps we suggest continuous batching but with a strict latency cap. Optimize will recommend the best batch size per route.

[14:05] Alex: price discussion — high level: Hosted is usage-based per token; Dedicated is reserved capacity w/ monthly commits. for your expected qps and SLA needs Dedicated probably makes sense. i'll send a pricing sketch.

[15:00] (Transcript artifact: speaker label sometimes says Speaker 2)
[15:20] Miguel: on quantization — does Redwood support 4-bit/8-bit and how do we measure quality loss?
[15:26] Sofia: yes we support 8-bit and selective 4-bit for certain models; Console's Optimize runs evals on your prompts and will show exact metric delta. you can also pin failure-critical routes to full precision.

[16:00] Alex: quick note on model fallbacks — you can set routing policies so if your preferred instance is saturated we fallback to a compatible variant (e.g., quantized vs full). this keeps availability up.

[17:10] Dana: curious about developer experience — SDKs, sample code.
[17:14] Sofia: we have REST + SDKs (python, node, go). sample repo includes schema examples and function adapters. we'll share the repo link after the call.

[18:00] (Minor crosstalk)
[18:20] Miguel: benchmark plan — we want to run a 50 qps synthetic run with a mix of short and long contexts and see 95th percentile latencies. can Redwood support that?
[18:27] Alex: yes we'll run it from our Dedicated cluster in region, or you can run it in your Private sandbox. we'll coordinate with Miguel.

[19:10] Sofia: another feature — structured reranking: we can ask the model to return multiple candidate objects and the runtime will run a lightweight reranker function that applies business rules before returning the top candidate. useful for financial reconciliation flows.
[19:40] Dana: nice. does that cost more?
[19:42] Sofia: you pay per token and per refine step; Optimize models cost tradeoffs for that too.

[20:00] (Transcript continues with example JSON snippets and a small typo: "K-V cache" occasionally spelled wrong)
[21:35] Leah: one more on compliance — data residency: can logs be kept only within eu-west-1 for us?
[21:41] Alex: yes Region-level data residency possible with Private or Dedicated with region pinning. logs and artifacts exported to your storage in-region.

[22:10] Sofia: showing the guardrails UI — you can set a schema enforcement policy per route, plus content filters and a hooks list for validators. here's a sample rule: if amount > 10000 then require CFO approval via manual sign-off before tool execution. That's a simple policy example.

[23:05] Miguel: will that manual sign-off be part of the realtime flow? we need to know how long hold states persist.
[23:11] Sofia: you can configure hold timeouts — typical pattern is 30 mins for manual holds with webhooks to notify your ops channel.

[24:00] (Short pause)
[24:22] Alex: let's walk through risk scenarios: if the model attempts to expose PII or leak tokens, our content scanner combined with registered KMS and audit logs can flag and either redact or block. we can supply examples in the security pack.

[25:40] Dana: okay looks good. final quick question: what's the onboarding timeline for a pilot?
[25:47] Alex: typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: initial kickoff, security review, small Dedicated allocation, and benchmark runs. full production tends to take longer depending on integrations.

[26:20] Miguel: for the benchmark we will need a small dedicated cluster and temporary credentials; who will own that?
[26:26] Alex: Redwood will provision the cluster; we'll need Miguel's IAM/KMS contact to set up the KMS bridge.

[27:00] Sofia: i just posted a link to the sample notebook in chat (link: https://redwood.example.com/samples/structured-output) — note: placeholder link.

[27:18] (Customer reads link)
[27:36] Dana: a few transcribe artifacts — sometimes product names get mangled; can you confirm the name of the console tab again?
[27:42] Sofia: it's "Optimize" in the Console and the guardrail UI is in "Policies".

[28:10] Alex: we're almost at the wrap. recap: we'll send Pilot pricing and Dedicated options; Sofia will send security docs; Miguel will share workload profile and prompts; Dana will confirm success criteria. we'll also schedule the benchmark for week of 2026-10-12.

[28:40] (Short clarifications)
[29:00] Dana: one last ask — sample SLA language for latency and uptime?
[29:05] Alex: yes will include sample SLA. Dedicated SLA covers 99.9% uptime and latency targets per route in the SOW.

[30:00] (Silence, then small wrap)
[31:12] Alex: ok thanks all. Sofia you want to add anything?
[31:15] Sofia: no, just that we'll also include a short runbook for rollback and canary. and we have automation to revert quantization changes if evals regress.

[31:35] Miguel: thanks, appreciate the time. we'll review docs and get back with constraint list.

[32:00] Leah: thanks everyone.

[47:10] (Call end voice)

Closing notes: agreed next steps and action items captured. References shared: security pack (link placeholder), sample repo (link placeholder), pricing sketch (to be sent).
